timeline_digest.summary: To obtain utterance start and end times, one option is to have transcribers provide them, though this may require specific software. An alternative is to use forced alignment to generate the timestamps later.

The annotation workflow will rely on automatically generated time marks derived from forced alignment of words, rather than requiring annotators to create them manually. Annotators will then classify the frames within these inherited time boundaries.

A proposed workflow for annotation involves automatically generating time marks for words using a method like forced alignment, which would then be used as boundaries for classifying the audio frames within them.

The specific technical method for automatically generating time marks for annotation is undecided, although it is agreed that it will be based on word alignments (e.g., via forced alignment) and handled by the engineering team.

The team decided that a solution for forced alignment must be found, as it is considered essential for attaching labels to words and enabling further analysis, and manual marking is not a viable alternative.

To address the critical need for word-level timings in the absence of a dedicated forced alignment tool, the team will experiment with using existing, albeit imperfect, aligners as a workaround. The plan is to test a 'very bad' aligner from the Broadcast News

The project lacks a forced alignment tool to generate word timings, which is considered an essential capability for attaching labels to words and enabling further analysis. The team must find a solution, as manual marking is too inefficient. A potential workar

A forced alignment tool is considered essential for attaching labels to words, but one is not available for the project. Without an automated aligner, word timings would have to be marked by hand, which is considered very inefficient and a blocker for many typ
The team decided that Brian will be the single point of contact for all issues related to IBM.
It is unclear whether IBM will still perform the forced alignment as was previously expected, as there has been no recent communication to confirm their commitment.
The group agreed that the speaker should contact Brian directly to discuss the proposal of running a forced alignment on a newly completed transcript to test the current overlap encoding method.
It is an open question whether it is feasible or desirable to perform forced alignment on newly completed transcripts, given the current method for encoding speaker overlaps.
A completed transcript could be used to test the current overlap encoding method by running a forced alignment experiment.
To address the imprecise timing of laughter tags in transcription, it was proposed that forced alignment could be used to more accurately place the event.

The established transcription workflow is to first segment audio into chunks, and then transcribe the words within those chunks. This process is performed before forced alignment, as it provides the necessary time-localized text required for the alignment.
Forced alignment requires time marks to determine where a transcribed word occurs in the audio signal.

A key technical challenge is that the IBM transcripts do not map words to audio segments. While forced alignment is a potential solution, it is difficult to apply to a long, unsegmented audio file. To make alignment work on pre-segmented audio, a word-to-segme

The solution to the transcript-to-audio alignment problem is currently dependent on IBM. It is unknown whether IBM can provide an initial forced alignment or has other useful transcription outputs, and this information needs to be confirmed with them.

The analysis process will be updated to require more precise start and end times for speech segments before running them through the recognizer for forced alignment. The time boundaries from this alignment will then be used to compute prosodic features.

Explore methods to improve forced alignment accuracy, including pre-processing for a better signal-to-noise ratio, using more precise time synchronization around speech segments, and applying global processing to the signal before segmentation.
The status of a specific system, referred to as 'the IBM one', is an open question relevant to the ongoing exploration of signal processing solutions.
A potential method to improve forced alignment is to apply global processing to the audio signal before it is segmented.
Forced alignment accuracy is negatively impacted by the amount of non-speech audio (e.g., silence) surrounding a target speech segment, leading to more errors.
A manual validation process will be implemented to assess the quality of forced alignments, where linguists will check the accuracy of the generated time boundaries.
Manually verify the quality of the forced alignments by having linguists or other qualified personnel check the correctness of the generated time boundaries.
Good quality forced alignments are valuable because they enable the extraction of information like prosody and speaker overlaps directly from the time-aligned transcriptions.

An evaluation method for word-level forced alignment accuracy needs to be established, as one has not yet been conducted. Proposed approaches include creating a detailed manual transcription with word boundaries for comparison, or having a linguist perform a q
A previous evaluation was conducted for speaker overlaps, but not for word-level forced alignment.
There is an open question on how to perform forced alignment for non-verbal vocalizations. An iterative approach has been suggested, which would require models for the spreading of acoustic features.
An iterative approach was suggested for performing forced alignment on non-verbal vocalizations.
Provide an update on the forced alignment results once they become available.
The proposed workflow of manually adjusting forced alignment results will not save time if the initial automatic results are of poor quality.
It is not yet known if the forced alignment process will work effectively on segments that contain a lot of pauses around the words.
A workflow was proposed where human transcribers would manually adjust the output of an automatic segmentation or forced alignment process, with the goal of saving time.
An experiment will be run using forced alignment on pre-segmented data to generate word boundaries. The pre-segmentations will be based on Jane's work at a specific threshold (e.g., level eight).
The team will generate 12 hours of force-aligned and recognized data by converting Jane's post-processed, channelized transcript into a reference for the recognizer using scripts.
As a condition for accepting the proposed workflow, the steps of the editing process need to be explained.
Continue working on improving forced alignment, which is currently failing in the presence of significant cross-talk. The current method using reject models is ineffective.

The forced alignment process is struggling with channels containing significant cross-talk. A scheme using reject models is frequently failing, often misaligning the beginning of the target speaker's utterance to the start of another speaker's speech. It is un
Initial experiments suggest that it may not be possible to obtain clean forced alignments from audio channels that contain significant amounts of cross-talk.

To measure speech overlap, the team will use forced alignments to report on actual temporal overlap, which is considered a more feasible and rigorous approach than a previous method based on signal correlation.
The performance of the forced alignment on non-lapel microphone data has not yet been evaluated.
It is uncertain whether the forced alignment process will perform adequately on lapel microphone data, and a decision needs to be made on whether to omit this step if the performance is poor.
A critical argument for the evaluation of the forced alignment process is that it must not produce false positives of speech, meaning it should not identify speech where none exists.

The primary justification for using forced alignment is to determine the start and end boundaries of speech on each channel, making intermediate word-level boundary accuracy a non-critical aspect for this specific application.
It is argued that if forced alignment proves ineffective for lapel microphone data, it should be omitted for that specific data source, implying that its use is contingent on performance.

The team will proceed with the existing data, which was transcribed before the improved interface with tightened boundaries was available, and will evaluate the difficulty of manually correcting alignment issues as they arise.

The transcription workflow has been updated with an improved interface. Transcribers will now start with pre-defined, tightened speech boundaries, which is expected to better constrain and improve the subsequent forced alignment process.

A decision is needed on how to process approximately 10 existing synchronous, non-time-tightened meeting recordings for the corpus. The original plan to use forced alignment is in doubt, and a fallback proposal is to 'fake' the alignment, which would introduce

Since forced alignment is not a reliable option for processing older synchronous recordings, a fallback strategy of 'faking' the alignment and accepting a 10-20% error rate is justified, as this may be sufficient for non-lapel microphone audio.
Consult with Brian Kingsbury on the feasibility and implementation of using forced alignment to clean up transcripts.
A method is needed to produce high-quality alignments for the initial set of meeting data, as the current alignments are not considered final and require a cleanup process.

The feasibility of using forced alignment to clean up and improve transcript alignments is an open question, with known complications related to speech overlap and lapel microphones that need to be addressed.
Forced alignment has been a long-standing proposal for cleaning up transcriptions, with the understanding that the output would always require human review and not be treated as the final version.

For forced alignment, the approach is changing from using unadapted models to using acoustic adaptation. The new strategy involves adapting the phone models to the specific speaker and adapting the reject model using speech from all other channels.
The current forced alignment process uses unadapted acoustic models.

To improve forced alignment quality, a new approach was implemented to address a common error where the first word of a recognition was misaligned to the earliest possible position. The solution involved two changes: reducing the severity of pruning and adding
Analyzing the types of errors occurring in forced alignments led to a definite improvement in the system's performance.

Although rescoring ASR results by excluding background speech regions yields better performance, the method used to identify these regions (forced alignment) is known to be error-prone, leaving open the question of how to perform this exclusion robustly.

The team will use two hand-adjusted meetings as reference data to fine-tune the forced alignment model. This hand-corrected data provides an objective measure to evaluate how well different model parameters align with the actual speech.
A decision is needed on whether to use the two hand-adjusted meetings to fine-tune the forced alignment model, which would provide an objective measure for alignment quality.

Hand-corrected meeting data is important for fine-tuning the forced alignment model because it provides an objective measure to evaluate how well different model parameters align the output to the actual speech.
The viability of using forced alignment to automatically detect transcription errors is uncertain, as the method requires a sufficient number of words in the transcript to be effective.
Propose using forced alignment on individual audio channels to automatically detect transcription errors, treating the 'beeps' that mark errors as words.

A proposal to simplify the alignment model to only use a general speech model and a beep model for verifying redaction beeps has been met with concern. It is uncertain whether this simplified forced alignment approach would be computationally feasible, as it m
A potential drawback of simplifying the alignment model to exclude words is that forced alignment could become extremely slow, possibly even slower than running a full recognition model.

Forced alignment for redaction beeps requires word content in addition to a beep model. A beep-only model would fail if the number of beeps in the audio and transcript differ, as it would sequentially align all detected beeps, resulting in incorrect offsets an

When using forced alignment to match segments instead of a beep model, the specific threshold or criteria for what constitutes a "failed" alignment, which would indicate a mismatch, has not yet been defined.

An alternative alignment method, used successfully in the past, was proposed to replace the beep model. This method uses forced alignment on extracted segments, requiring a text transcript as a model. A low likelihood score indicates a failed alignment and a m

Forced alignment can be used as an alternative to a beep model for segment alignment, but this approach has a significant tradeoff: while it has been successful in the past, it will result in some incorrect segment endpoints that require manual correction.
A known drawback of using forced alignment for segmenting audio without explicit endpoint markers (like beeps) is that some segment boundaries will be inaccurate and require manual correction.

Using word-level features derived from forced alignment, such as word frequency and backchannel identification, is considered a form of 'cheating' in the current classifiers because it relies on ground truth words, which would not be available in a real applic

The team agreed to conduct a new experiment: use tandem features to generate SRI forced alignments, and then use these new alignments to retrain the neural network model. The goal of this process is to optimize the model for word error rate.
The team will retrain the neural net using SRI forced alignments generated from tandem features. This experiment aims to optimize the system for word error rate.
Use forced alignment to help transcribe the large volume of digit-reading data.
Forced alignment alone is considered insufficient for transcribing the digit-reading data due to the presence of speaker self-corrections in the recordings.

An unresolved question exists on the best method for transcribing digits to get a 'clean' set. The options are forced alignment against the known script versus using a speech recognizer. The core uncertainty is whether the error rate from speaker mistakes is h

Speakers make mistakes and have false starts when reading digits, meaning the script used for forced alignment may be incorrect. The rate of these speaker errors is a critical factor when comparing the accuracy of forced alignment against a speech recognizer.

The Transcriber tool demo was updated to use forced alignments, presenting text as word-level segments instead of long chunks. This was implemented via a conversion script that transforms an aligner's SRT output into the required Transcriber XML format, avoidi

Using forced alignments increases the number of segments in the transcript file, which makes the Transcriber tool significantly slower to load because it does not handle a large number of segments well.

It is possible to integrate forced alignment data into the Transcriber tool without modifying the software itself, by using external conversion scripts to format the input XML correctly from a source like an SRT file.
After Quicknet can read SRI-format feature files, generate the necessary Pfiles.

The team adopted a new method for creating and scoring a reference transcript by force-aligning and merging individual transcriber outputs. The initial scoring approach will evaluate only non-overlapped, single-speaker speech.
It is an open question how to score a merged reference transcript created from force-aligning individual transcriber outputs, especially given that the forced alignments are not perfect.
To create a reference transcript, a proposed method is to force-align individual transcriber transcripts and then merge them in time.

Despite the known issue of imperfect forced alignments, the proposed method for generating a reference transcript is worth trying as it is expected to be a significant improvement over the current process.
The existing speech recognition models are gender-dependent, requiring at least gender detection to function correctly.
A new large digit corpus will be created by running forced alignment on the large number of existing, untranscribed digit recordings.

The creation of a large digit corpus using forced alignment on existing recordings is a desired goal, but it is currently blocked as the identified person to lead the project, Dave Gelbart, is unavailable.

The MATE document is a broad comparison of existing text mark-up submissions, which includes the Text Encoding Initiative (TEI).

timeline_digest.summary: Training a recognizer requires tens of hours of labeled data, which poses a significant and unresolved resource challenge for the project.

The MARSEC project is proposed as a potential source of training data, as it contains time-aligned spoken data with rich intonational and stress-oriented transcription, a combination not often found together.
